key_terms.meaning: Using several execution units at once so a job finishes sooner or a bigger job becomes possible
Widening the word from 8 to 32 or 64 bits so one instruction moves more bits at a time
Pipelining and multiple issue let independent machine instructions overlap in one core
A four-way classification by number of instruction streams against number of data streams
Single instruction stream, multiple data streams; one control unit drives many identical lanes
Multiple instruction streams, multiple data streams; every processor runs its own code
Execution is triggered by the arrival of operands rather than by a program counter
All processors see one address space and talk through ordinary load and store instructions
Each node has private memory; nodes exchange data only by sending messages
Parallel Random Access Machine: ideal shared memory, unit-cost access, lockstep steps
PRAM sub-models that forbid, or allow, several processors reading one cell in the same step
Number of links attached to one node; it fixes the wiring cost per node
Largest number of links on the shortest path between any two nodes
Smallest number of links cut when the nodes are split into two equal halves
d-dimensional cube network with 2^d nodes, degree d, diameter d, and one link per bit flipped
Log-stage network built from 2×2 switches, giving diameter log₂ N and a perfect-shuffle wiring between stages
S(p) = T₁ / T(p), the one-processor time divided by the time on p processors
E(p) = S(p) / p, the fraction of processor capacity actually turned into speedup
Spreading tasks over processors so the latest finishing processor waits as little as possible
The same operation is applied to different slices of the data held on different devices
One model is cut into parts, and different devices hold and compute different parts

takeaways: Time and problem size are the two pressures that push computing from one core to many.
Flynn's four boxes are a coarse label: SISD, SIMD, MISD and MIMD; almost every modern server is MIMD.
Shared memory is easy to program and hard to scale; distributed memory scales and forces you to think in messages.
PRAM is not a machine you buy, it is a measuring stick for how much parallelism an algorithm really contains.
An interconnection network is a set of trade-offs: more links per node buys a smaller diameter at a higher wiring cost.
Speedup is bounded by the sequential part of the code, so efficiency falls as you add processors beyond the useful point.
Good decomposition plus good mapping beats a faster machine on a badly split problem.
Data parallelism splits the work, model parallelism splits the network; large training jobs usually need both.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are usually asked as compare-and-contrast plus a worked numeric part, so define each model, draw its network or block diagram, and finish with degree, diameter, bisection width or a speedup calculation.

bank.q: State Flynn's taxonomy. Describe SISD, SIMD, MISD and MIMD with one machine or use case for each, and explain why MISD is rare in practice.
outline: Two axes: instruction streams and data streams
SISD: one core, one instruction at a time
SIMD: array processor, GPU lane, vector unit; one control unit, many ALUs
MIMD: multicore server, cluster; each processor has its own program counter
MISD: systolic array as the usual example; no general-purpose machine of this kind

bank.q: Compare shared-memory and distributed-memory parallel architectures under the headings address space, communication mechanism, synchronisation cost, scalability and programming model.
outline: One address space versus private memories per node
Load/store versus send and receive primitives
Cache coherence and bus traffic versus explicit messages
Scalability limits of a common bus and memory
OpenMP/pthreads versus MPI
Hybrid clusters use both levels

bank.q: Define PRAM and describe its EREW, CREW, ERCW and CRCW variants, giving the conflict rule for each.
outline: Unbounded processors, unit-cost shared cell access, lockstep steps
EREW: exclusive read, exclusive write
CREW: concurrent read, exclusive write
ERCW: exclusive read, concurrent write
CRCW with common, arbitrary, priority or combining write rules
Stronger models are more powerful in theory and harder to build

bank.q: Define speedup and efficiency. State Amdahl's law and explain what it says about the limit of parallel speedup.
outline: S(p) = T₁/T(p) with T₁ the best one-processor time
E(p) = S(p)/p
Amdahl: S ≤ 1/(s + (1−s)/p) where s is the serial fraction
Limit 1/s as p grows
Superlinear speedup from cache or search effects

bank.q: Explain the need for parallel processing and list the levels of parallelism from bit level to job level with one example each.
outline: Power and clock limits ending the free speedup era
Bit level: 64-bit adders
Instruction level: pipelining, superscalar
Data level: vector units, GPU lanes
Thread and task level: multicore OpenMP
Job level: cluster and grid batches

bank.q: A program takes 200 s on one processor. On 8 processors it takes 32 s. Find speedup and efficiency. If 10 s of the parallel time is unavoidable serial work, recompute the best possible speedup with 8 and with 64 processors.
outline: E(8) = 6.25/8 = 0.78, that is 78 percent
Serial fraction s = 10/200 = 0.05
Ceiling 1/s = 20 regardless of p

bank.q: For a hypercube of dimension d, derive the number of nodes, degree, diameter, link count and bisection width. Repeat for a 2-D mesh of side 2^(d/2).
outline: Hypercube: N = 2^d nodes, degree d, diameter d, links = d·2^(d−1)
Bisection width of hypercube = 2^(d−1)
Mesh with N nodes: degree 4, diameter 2(√N − 1)
Mesh link count = 2N − 2√N
Mesh bisection width = √N
Compare which is better for the same N

bank.q: A 512×512 matrix is multiplied by itself. Show how to decompose the work into tasks, and compute how many tasks you get with a block size of 64×64.
outline: Standard triple loop cost O(N³)
Block decomposition: 8×8 blocks of size 64
512/64 = 8 blocks per side, so 64 block rows and 64 output blocks
Each output block needs 8 multiplications of 64×64 blocks
Choose owner-computes rule
Load balance is even when block size divides N

bank.q: An engineer must train a model that does not fit on one GPU. Explain how data parallelism and model parallelism would each be applied, and sketch a combined plan.
outline: Data parallelism: replicate model, split each mini-batch, all-reduce gradients
Bottleneck: each device must still hold full weights and activations
Model parallelism: split layers, pipeline micro-batches, send activations between devices
Bottleneck: idle bubbles and communication volume
Combined: pipeline across groups, data parallel within a group
Trade-off: batch size, per-device memory, interconnect bandwidth

bank.q: Simulate one PRAM variant on another. Show how an EREW PRAM simulates a CREW step in O(log p) steps and explain what that costs.
outline: CREW lets many processors read the same cell
Use a binary tree of reads rooted at one processor
log₂ p steps to broadcast the value back
Total slowdown O(log p)
CRCW simulation needs priority or sorting work
Conclusion: model strength converts to a logarithmic factor

bank.q: Compare a tree network, a mesh and a hypercube for 1024 processors. Which do you choose for a fast Fourier transform workload and why?
outline: Tree: degree 3, diameter 2 log N, narrow bisection width 1
Mesh: constant degree 4, diameter 2(√N − 1), bisection √N
Hypercube: degree and diameter log₂ N = 10, bisection 512
FFT needs a butterfly or shuffle pattern of communication
Tree links saturate at the root
Justify hypercube or butterfly on bisection width and diameter

bank.q: Discuss the causes of load imbalance in a parallel program. Compare static and dynamic load balancing with one example of each.
outline: Causes: unequal task size, data-dependent work, synchronisation, heterogeneous nodes
Static: tasks fixed before the run; cheap, good when work is predictable
Example: equal blocks in dense matrix multiply
Dynamic: work queue or work stealing; example ray tracing, branch-and-bound
Cost of task migration and scheduling overhead
Measure with per-processor busy time and idle time

bank.q: Examine how the level of parallelism you exploit changes the achievable speedup, from bit level to job level. Use Amdahl's law and the idea of parallel overhead in your answer.
outline: Each level removes a different bottleneck
Bit and instruction level give a small fixed factor
Data and thread level give large factors but need shared data
Job level adds network and scheduling overhead
Amdahl limit for a fixed serial fraction
Gustafson's view: scaled problem size keeps efficiency high
Overheads grow with p, so efficiency drops

glossary.def: Doing several pieces of work at the same time on separate hardware units.
Several activities that may overlap in time but need not run on separate hardware.
A single processor executing one instruction stream on one data stream, the classical von Neumann machine.
One instruction stream applied to many data items at once.
Independent processors each running their own instruction stream on their own data.
A computation style in which an instruction fires as soon as its input values arrive.
Uniform Memory Access: every processor reaches every memory word in about the same time.
Non-Uniform Memory Access: a processor reaches its local memory faster than remote memory.
Communication in which one process sends a buffer and another process receives it.
The rule that keeps copies of a memory word in several caches consistent.
One round in which every processor reads, computes and writes in lockstep.
Concurrent Read, Concurrent Write: several processors may write one cell in a step, under a stated rule.
The set of links and switches that moves data between processors or between processors and memory.
One processor with its memory and its network connection point.
A single communication channel joining two nodes.
Choosing the path a message follows through a network.
A fixed permutation that splits the address bits and interleaves them, used between butterfly stages.
A hypercube in which each node is replaced by a cycle, giving constant degree and logarithmic diameter.
Every node joined directly to every other; degree N−1 and diameter 1.
How well performance keeps growing as processors and problem size increase together.
The speedup bound set by the serial fraction of the program.
The amount of computation in one task; coarse grain means few large tasks.
The step of breaking a problem into tasks that can run independently.
The step of assigning tasks to processors so that work and communication stay balanced.
Speedup larger than p, usually from extra cache or a search that prunes more work.
A collective in which every process ends with the same combined value, such as a summed gradient.
